mentions.context: Empirical research on quality de- fects in natural language requirements relies heavily on datasets, ideally as realistic and representative as possible.
This paper introduces QURE (Quality in Requirements), a new dataset comprising 2,111 industrial requirements that have been annotated through a real-world review process.

Our goal is to foster transparency, comparability, and empirical rigor by supporting the development of a common gold standard for requirements quality datasets.
The quality of natural language (NL) requirements is im- portant for efficient and effective software and systems engi- neering , .
Deficiencies such as ambiguity, inconsistency, and incompleteness in requirements can lead to significant challenges, including increased development costs and project delays .
Recognizing these challenges, the research commu- nity has extensively explored methods to detect and mitigate quality issues in NL requirements .
For instance, the con- cept of \"requirements smells\" has been introduced to identify patterns indicative of potential quality problems, facilitating rapid quality assurance processes .
Despite the substantial body of research, publicly available datasets that provide NL requirements annotated with quality- related labels are scarce.
Moreover, the absence of standardized datasets  impedes the advancement of empirical studies aimed at un- derstanding and improving the quality of requirements .
To address this gap, we present QURE (Quality in Requirements), a comprehensive dataset consisting of 2,111 NL requirements sampled from real-world automotive projects.

We also provide an in-depth discussion on the labeling taxonomy, dataset provenance, and annotation quality, contributing to a more standardized and empirical approach to requirements quality assessment.
By making this dataset publicly available, we aim to sup- port empirical research on the quality of natural language requirements.
In addition, the real-world industrial context of the data enhances its validity, offering researchers and practitioners a more realistic basis to evaluate techniques and understand quality defects.
Ultimately, this contribution supports the development of more reliable, scalable, and context-sensitive approaches to improving the quality of requirements across diverse domains.

The motivation of Krisch's underlying research - was to create rules to identify quality defects in natural language requirements, in particular from a tester's perspec- tive.
The categories of problem candidates (now often referred to as requirements smells ) included weak words, passive voice, or ambiguous references .

The released QURE dataset contains 2,111 unique require- ments in natural, unconstrained English.
Weak words signal potential defects in requirements.

For example, in the requirement \"If the button is pressed for a long  time, then ...\", the word \"long\" is problematic, whereas in \"The long range radar shall send ...\", the same word is appropriate in that context and, therefore, not considered a defect.
Most requirements appear only once in the dataset, but some have multiple weak words.
A total of 633 requirements, almost a third, are labeled as defect while 1,478 requirements are labeled as ok despite the weak word.

In our early examination, synthetic requirements often ex- hibit a noticeably lower degree of realism.
One plausible explanation for this is that LLMs are more frequently trained on simplified, textbook-style examples than on full-fledged, domain-specific requirements documents.
We do not claim that generating realistic requirements with LLMs is impossible.
Rather, our findings suggest that gener- ating representative and realistic synthetic requirements is not straightforward.
Addressing the question of whether, and under what  conditions, LLMs can be used to generate high-quality, real- istic requirements remains a compelling direction for future research.
